{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
{{Short description|Canonical connection on a pseudo-Riemannian manifold}}
[[File:Parallel_transport_sphere.svg|right|thumb|A connection on the sphere rolls the tangent plane from one point to another. As it does so, the point of contact traces out a curve in the plane: the [[Development (differential geometry)|development]].]]
In [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian]] or [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold|pseudo-Riemannian geometry]] (in particular the [[Lorentzian manifold|Lorentzian geometry]] of [[general relativity]]), the '''Levi-Civita connection''' is the unique [[affine connection]] on the [[tangent bundle]] of a [[manifold]] that [[metric connection|preserves]] the ([[pseudo-Riemannian manifold|pseudo-]])[[Riemannian metric]] and is [[Torsion (differential geometry)|torsion]]-free. The [[fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry]] states that there is a unique connection that satisfies these properties.

The connection formalizes and generalizes the "rolling without slipping or twisting" method of transporting tangent planes of a smooth surface embedded in <math>\R^3</math> (or generally, any Riemannian manifold, by the [[Nash embedding theorems]]).

The [[covariant derivative]] is defined given any affine connection. In the theory of [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian]] and [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]]s, the "covariant derivative" by default refers to the one defined using the Levi-Civita connection. The components (structure coefficients) of this connection with respect to a system of local coordinates are called [[Christoffel symbols]].

== History ==
The Levi-Civita connection is named after [[Tullio Levi-Civita]], although originally "discovered" by [[Elwin Bruno Christoffel]]. Levi-Civita,<ref name="Levi-Civita1917">
{{Cite journal|author-link=Tullio Levi-Civita|year=1917|title=Nozione di parallelismo in una varietà qualunque|trans-title=The notion of parallelism on any manifold|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1428456|journal=[[Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo]]|language=it|volume=42|pages=173–205|doi=10.1007/BF03014898|jfm=46.1125.02|author-first=Tullio|author-last=Levi-Civita|s2cid=122088291}}
</ref> along with [[Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro]], used Christoffel's symbols<ref>{{cite journal |title=Ueber die Transformation der homogenen Differentialausdrücke zweiten Grades |lang=de|trans-title=On transformations of homogeneous differential forms of degree two|last=Christoffel|first=Elwin B.|author-link=Elwin Bruno Christoffel|journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]]|volume=70|pages=46–70(part 1),241–245(part 2)|year=1869|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_journal-fuer-die-reine-und-angewandte-mathematik_1869_70/page/46|via=[[Internet Archive]]|id={{JFM|02.0128.03}}, {{JFM|02.0129.01}}. {{ARK|ark:/13960/t5q93c802}}|doi=10.1515/crll.1869.70.46|s2cid=122999847}}</ref> to define the notion of [[parallel transport]] and explore the relationship of parallel transport with the [[Riemann curvature tensor|curvature]], thus developing the modern notion of [[holonomy]].<ref>See {{cite book|first=Michael|last=Spivak|author-link=Michael Spivak | title=A Comprehensive introduction to differential geometry (Volume II)|publisher=Publish or Perish Press|year=1999|isbn=0-914098-71-3 |page=238 }}</ref>

In 1869, Christoffel discovered that the components of the intrinsic derivative of a vector field, upon changing the coordinate system, transform as the components of a contravariant vector. This discovery was the real beginning of tensor analysis. 

In 1906, [[L. E. J. Brouwer]] was the first [[mathematician]] to consider the [[parallel transport]] of a [[Euclidean vector|vector]] for the case of 
a space of [[constant curvature]].<ref>
{{Cite journal|author-link=L. E. J. Brouwer|year=1906|title=Het krachtveld der niet-Euclidische, negatief gekromde ruimten|journal=Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen. Verslagen|volume=15|pages=75–94|author-first=L. E. J.|author-last=Brouwer}}
</ref><ref>
{{Cite journal|year=1906|title=The force field of the non-Euclidean spaces with negative curvature|journal=Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen. Proceedings|volume=9|pages=116–133|author-first=L. E. J.|author-last=Brouwer|bibcode=1906KNAB....9..116B}}
</ref>

In 1917, [[Tullio Levi-Civita]] pointed out its importance for the case of a [[hypersurface]] immersed in a [[Euclidean space]], i.e., for the case of a [[Riemannian manifold]] embedded in a "larger" ambient space.<ref name="Levi-Civita1917" /> He interpreted the intrinsic derivative in the case of an embedded surface as the tangential component of the usual derivative in the ambient affine space. The Levi-Civita notions of [[intrinsic derivative]] and parallel displacement of a vector along a curve make sense on an abstract Riemannian manifold, even though the original motivation relied on a specific embedding <math>M^n \subset \mathbf{R}^{n(n+1)/2}.</math>

In 1918, independently of Levi-Civita, [[Jan Arnoldus Schouten]] obtained analogous results.<ref>

== Notation ==
* {{math|(''M'', ''g'')}} denotes a [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]].
* {{math|''TM''}} is the [[tangent bundle]] of {{math|''M''}}.
* {{math|''g''}} is the [[pseudo-Riemannian metric]] of {{math|''M''}}.
* {{math|''X'', ''Y'', ''Z''}} are smooth vector fields on {{math|''M''}}, i. e. smooth [[section (fiber bundle)|section]]s of {{math|''TM''}}.
* {{math|[''X'', ''Y'']}} is the [[Lie bracket of vector fields|Lie bracket]] of {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}}. It is again a smooth vector field.

The metric {{math|''g''}} can take up to two vectors or vector fields {{math|''X'', ''Y''}} as arguments. In the former case the output is a number, the (pseudo-)[[inner product]] of {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}}. In the latter case, the inner product of {{math|''X''<sub>''p''</sub>, ''Y''<sub>''p''</sub>}} is taken at all points {{math|''p''}} on the manifold so that {{math|''g''(''X'', ''Y'')}} defines a smooth function on {{math|''M''}}. Vector fields act (by definition) as differential operators on smooth functions. In local coordinates <math>(x_1,\ldots, x_n) </math>, the action reads
: <math>X(f) = X^i\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}f = X^i\partial_i f</math>
where [[Albert Einstein|Einstein's]] [[Einstein summation convention|summation convention]] is used.

== Formal definition ==
An [[affine connection]] <math>\nabla</math> is called a Levi-Civita connection if
# ''it preserves the metric'', i.e., <math>\nabla g = 0 </math>.
# ''it is [[torsion of connection|torsion]]-free'', i.e., for any vector fields <math>X</math>  and <math>Y</math> we have <math>\nabla_X Y - \nabla_Y X = [X,Y]</math>, where <math>[X, Y]</math> is the [[Lie bracket of vector fields|Lie bracket]] of the [[vector field]]s <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>.

Condition 1 above is sometimes referred to as [[compatibility with the metric]], and condition 2 is sometimes called symmetry, cf. Do Carmo's text.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Carmo |first=Manfredo Perdigão do |title=Riemannian geometry |date=1992 |publisher=Birkhäuser |others=Francis J. Flaherty |isbn=0-8176-3490-8 |location=Boston |oclc=24667701}}</ref>

== Fundamental theorem of (pseudo-)Riemannian geometry ==
{{main|Fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry}}
'''Theorem''' Every pseudo-Riemannian manifold <math>(M,g)</math> has a unique Levi-Civita connection <math>\nabla</math>.

''Proof'':<ref>{{cite book|title=Introduction to Riemannian manifolds|author=John M Lee|publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=2018|page=22}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Barrett O'Neill|title=Semi-Riemannian geometry with Applications to relativity|publisher=Academic Press|year=1983|page=61}}</ref>
To prove uniqueness, unravel the definition of the action of a connection on tensors to find 
: <math> X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr) = (\nabla_X g)(Y, Z) + g(\nabla_X Y, Z) + g( Y, \nabla_X Z)</math>.
Hence one can write the condition that <math>\nabla</math> preserves the metric as
: <math> X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr) =  g(\nabla_X Y, Z) + g( Y, \nabla_X Z)</math>.
By the symmetry of <math>g</math>,
: <math> X \bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr) + Y \bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr) - Z \bigl(g(Y,X)\bigr) = g(\nabla_X Y + \nabla_Y X, Z) + g(\nabla_X Z - \nabla_Z X, Y) + g(\nabla_Y Z - \nabla_Z Y, X)</math>.
By torsion-freeness, the right hand side is therefore equal to
: <math> 2g(\nabla_X Y, Z) - g([X,Y], Z) + g([X,Z], Y) + g([Y,Z], X)</math>.
Thus, the [[Jean-Louis_Koszul|Koszul]] formula
: <math> g(\nabla_X Y, Z) =  \tfrac{1}{2} \Big\{ X \bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr) + Y \bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr) - Z \bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr) + g([X,Y],Z) - g([Y,Z], X) - g([X,Z], Y) \Big\}</math>
holds. Hence, if a Levi-Civita connection exists, it must be unique, because <math>Z</math> is arbitrary, <math>g</math> is non degenerate, and the right hand side does not depend on <math>\nabla</math>. 

To prove existence, note that for given vector field <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>, the right hand side of the Koszul expression is linear over smooth functions in the vector field <math>Z</math>, not just real-linear. Hence by the non degeneracy of <math>g</math>, the right hand side uniquely defines some new vector field, which is suggestively denoted <math>\nabla_X Y</math> as in the left hand side. By substituting the Koszul formula, one now checks that for all vector fields <math>X, Y,Z</math> and all functions <math>f</math>,
: <math> g(\nabla_X (Y_1 + Y_2), Z) = g(\nabla_X Y_1, Z) + g(\nabla_X Y_2 , Z) </math>
: <math> g(\nabla_X (f Y), Z) = X(f) g(Y, Z) + f g(\nabla_X Y,Z) </math>
: <math> g(\nabla_X Y, Z) + g(\nabla_X Z, Y) =  X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)</math>
: <math> g(\nabla_X Y, Z) - g(\nabla_Y X, Z) = g([X,Y], Z). </math>
Hence the Koszul expression does, in fact, define a connection, and this connection is compatible with the metric and is torsion free, i.e. is a Levi-Civita connection.

With minor variation, the same proof shows that there is a unique connection that is compatible with the metric and has prescribed torsion.

== Christoffel symbols ==
Let <math>\nabla</math> be an affine connection on the tangent bundle. Choose local coordinates <math>x^1, \ldots, x^n</math> with coordinate basis vector fields <math>\partial_1, \ldots, \partial_n</math> and write <math>\nabla_j</math> for <math>\nabla_{\partial_j}</math>. The [[Christoffel symbols]] <math>\Gamma^l_{jk}</math> of <math>\nabla</math> with respect to these coordinates are defined as
: <math> \nabla_j\partial_k = \Gamma^l_{jk} \partial_l </math>

The Christoffel symbols conversely define the connection <math>\nabla</math> on the coordinate neighbourhood because
: <math>
\begin{align}
\nabla_X Y &=  \nabla_{X^j\partial_j} (Y^k \partial_k)
           \\&=  X^j\nabla_j(Y^k\partial_k)
           \\ &= X^j\bigl(\partial_j(Y^k)\partial_k + Y^k\nabla_j\partial_k\bigr) 
           \\ &= X^j\bigl(\partial_j(Y^k)\partial_k + Y^k\Gamma^l_{jk}\partial_l\bigr)
           \\ &= X^j\bigl(\partial_j(Y^l) + Y^k\Gamma^l_{jk}\bigr)\partial_l
\end{align}
</math>
that is,
: <math> (\nabla_j Y)^l = \partial_jY^l + \Gamma^l_{jk} Y^k </math>
An affine connection <math>\nabla</math> is compatible with a metric iff
: <math> \partial_i \bigl(g(\partial_j, \partial_k) \bigr)
                         = g(\nabla_i\partial_j, \partial_k) + g(\partial_j, \nabla_i\partial_k)
                         = g(\Gamma^l_{ij}\partial_l, \partial_k) + g(\partial_j, \Gamma_{ik}^l\partial_l)
                         
</math>
i.e., if and only if
: <math> \partial_i g_{jk} = \Gamma^l_{ij}g_{lk} + \Gamma^l_{ik}g_{jl}.</math>
An affine connection {{math|∇}} is torsion free iff
: <math>\nabla_j\partial_k - \nabla_k \partial_j = (\Gamma^l_{jk} - \Gamma^l_{kj})\partial_l = [\partial_j, \partial_k]= 0. </math>
i.e., if and only if 
: <math>\Gamma^l_{jk} = \Gamma^l_{kj}</math>
is symmetric in its lower two indices.

As one checks by taking for <math>X, Y, Z</math>, coordinate vector fields <math>\partial_j, \partial_k, \partial_l</math> (or computes directly), the Koszul expression of the Levi-Civita connection derived above is equivalent to a definition of the Christoffel symbols in terms of the metric as
: <math>\Gamma^l_{jk} = \tfrac{1}{2} g^{lr} \left( \partial _k g_{rj} + \partial _j g_{rk} - \partial _r g_{jk} \right)</math>
where as usual <math>g^{ij}</math> are the coefficients of the dual metric tensor, i.e. the entries of the inverse of the matrix <math>g_{kl}</math>.

== Derivative along curve ==
The Levi-Civita connection (like any affine connection)  also defines a derivative along [[curve]]s, sometimes denoted by <math>D</math>.

Given a smooth curve <math>\gamma</math> on <math>(M,g)</math> and a [[vector field]] <math>V</math> along <math>\gamma</math> its derivative is defined by
<math display="block">D_tV=\nabla_{\dot\gamma(t)}V.</math>

Formally, <math>D</math> is the [[pullback (differential geometry)|pullback connection]] <math>\gamma^*\nabla</math> on the [[pullback bundle]] <math>\gamma^*TM</math>.

In particular, <math>\dot\gamma(t)</math> is a vector field along the curve <math>\gamma</math> itself. If <math>\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}(t)}\dot{\gamma}(t)</math> vanishes, the curve is called a geodesic of the covariant derivative. Formally, the condition can be restated as the vanishing of the pullback connection applied to <math>\dot\gamma</math>:
<math display="block">\left(\gamma^*\nabla\right) \dot{\gamma}\equiv 0.</math>

If the covariant derivative is the Levi-Civita connection of a certain metric, then the geodesics for the connection are precisely those [[geodesics]] of the [[Metric tensor|metric]] that are parametrised proportionally to their arc length.

== Parallel transport ==
In general, [[parallel transport]] along a curve with respect to a connection defines [[isomorphism|isomorphisms]] between the tangent spaces at the points of the curve. If the connection is a Levi-Civita connection, then these isomorphisms are [[Orthogonal group|orthogonal]] – that is, they preserve the inner products on the various tangent spaces.

The images below show parallel transport induced by the Levi-Civita connection associated to two different Riemannian metrics on the [[punctured plane]] <math>\mathbf R^2 \backslash \{0,0\}</math>. The curve the parallel transport is done along is the unit circle. In [[Polar coordinate system|polar coordinates]], the metric on the left is the standard [[Riemannian_manifold#Euclidean_space|Euclidean metric]] <math>ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 = dr^2 + r^2 d\theta^2</math>, while the metric on the right is <math>ds^2 = dr^2 + d\theta^2</math>. The first metric extends to the entire plane, but the second metric has a singularity at the origin:
: <math>dr = \frac{xdx + ydy}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}</math>
: <math>d\theta = \frac{xdy - ydx}{x^2 + y^2}</math>
: <math>dr^2 + d\theta^2 = \frac{(xdx + ydy)^2}{x^2+y^2} + \frac{(xdy - ydx)^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}</math>.

== Example: the unit sphere in R<sup>3</sup> ==
Let {{math|⟨ , ⟩}} be the usual [[scalar product]] on {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}}. Let {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}} be the [[unit sphere]] in {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}}. The tangent space to {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}} at a point {{math|''m''}} is naturally identified with the vector subspace of {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}} consisting of all vectors orthogonal to {{math|''m''}}. It follows that a vector field {{math|''Y''}} on {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}} can be seen as a map {{math|''Y'' : '''S'''<sup>2</sup> → '''R'''<sup>3</sup>}}, which satisfies
<math display="Block">\bigl\langle Y(m), m\bigr\rangle = 0, \qquad \forall m\in \mathbf{S}^2.</math>

Denote as {{math|''d<sub>m</sub>Y''}} the differential of the map {{math|''Y''}} at the point {{math|''m''}}. Then we have:

{{math theorem|name=Lemma|math_statement= The formula
<math display="block">\left(\nabla_X Y\right)(m) = d_mY(X(m)) + \langle X(m),Y(m)\rangle m</math>
defines an affine connection on {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}} with vanishing torsion.}}

{{math proof|proof= It is straightforward to prove that {{math|∇}} satisfies the Leibniz identity and is {{math|''C''<sup>∞</sup>('''S'''<sup>2</sup>)}} linear in the first variable. It is also a straightforward computation to show that this connection is torsion free. So all that needs to be proved here is that the formula above produces a vector field tangent to {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}}. That is, we need to prove that for all {{math|''m''}} in {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}}
<math display="block">\bigl\langle\left(\nabla_X Y\right)(m),m\bigr\rangle = 0\qquad (1).</math>
Consider the map {{math|''f''}} that sends every {{math|''m''}} in {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}} to {{math|⟨''Y''(''m''), ''m''⟩}}, which is always 0. The map {{math|''f''}} is constant, hence its differential vanishes. In particular
<math display="block">d_mf(X) = \bigl\langle d_m Y(X),m\bigr\rangle + \bigl\langle Y(m), X(m)\bigr\rangle = 0.</math>
The equation (1) above follows. [[Q.E.D.]]}}

In fact, this connection is the Levi-Civita connection for the metric on {{math|'''S'''<sup>2</sup>}} inherited from {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}}. Indeed, one can check that this connection preserves the metric.

== Behaviour under conformal rescaling ==
If the metric <math>g</math> in a [[conformal geometry|conformal class]] is replaced by the conformally rescaled metric of the same class <math>\hat g=e^{2\gamma}g</math>, then the Levi-Civita connection transforms according to the rule<ref>{{cite book|author=Arthur Besse|title=Einstein manifolds|year=1987|publisher=Springer|page=58}}</ref>
<math display="block">\widehat\nabla_X Y = \nabla_XY + X(\gamma)Y + Y(\gamma)X - g(X,Y)\mathrm{grad}_g(\gamma).</math>
where <math>\mathrm{grad}_g(\gamma)</math> is the gradient vector field of <math>\gamma</math> i.e. the vector field <math>g</math>-dual to <math>d\gamma</math>, in local coordinates given by <math>g^{ik}(\partial_i \gamma)\partial_k</math>. Indeed, it is trivial to verify that <math>\widehat\nabla</math> is torsion-free.  To verify metricity, assume that <math>g(Y,Y)</math> is constant.  In that case,
<math display="block">\hat g(\widehat\nabla_XY,Y) = X(\gamma)\hat g(Y,Y) = \frac12 X(\hat g(Y,Y)).</math>

As an application, consider again the unit sphere, but this time under [[stereographic projection]], so that the metric (in complex [[Fubini–Study metric|Fubini–Study coordinates]] <math>z,\bar z</math>) is:
<math display="block">g = \frac{4\,dz\,d\bar z}{(1+z\bar z)^2}.</math>
This exhibits the metric of the sphere as conformally flat, with the Euclidean metric <math>dz\,d\bar z</math>, with  <math>\gamma = \ln(2)-\ln (1+z\bar z)</math>.  We have <math>d\gamma = -(1+z\bar z)^{-1}(\bar z\, dz + z\,d{\bar z})</math>, and so
<math display="block">\widehat\nabla_{\partial_z}\partial_z =  -\frac{2\bar z\partial_z}{1+z\bar z}.</math>
With the Euclidean gradient <math>\mathrm{grad}_{Euc}(\gamma) = -(1+z\bar z)^{-1}(\bar z\partial_z + z\partial_{\bar z})</math>, we have
<math display="block">\widehat\nabla_{\partial_z}\partial_{\bar z} =  0.</math>
These relations, together with their complex conjugates, define the Christoffel symbols for the two-sphere.
